The Hidden Curriculum

Who owns school, who writes what is taught, and what it is training you for. One story, told on the map from the top of the system down: who steers the world's schools, what governments use them for, who supplies them, who owns them, and who is paid at each step.

About this map
Method and sources
On the map

About This Map

Almost everyone on earth spends about twelve years in school, starting at an age when they believe what they are told. This map is about who decides what happens there, and where it is leading.

The term hidden curriculum comes from the study of schools. It means what school teaches without saying so: to sit still, to wait for permission, to accept a ranking, to want the next certificate. This map follows the organisations behind that: who writes the book, who sets the test, who owns the school and the company that sells it its laptops, who lends the government the money, and who sells the degree at the end.

One Story, Told From the Top Down

The main thing on the map is a single story in seven parts and 26 chapters. It treats the school system like an empire and maps its chain of command from the top down. Part 1 is the top: the international bodies that hold the shared plan, the money and the scoreboard. Part 2 is the national government, and what it uses school for. Part 3 is the suppliers who write the rules, the lessons and the tests. Part 4 is the owners of the schools. Part 5 is the software that records pupils. Part 6 is what is sold when school ends. Part 7 is where people pushed back. Each layer behaves as it does because of the layer above it, so each chapter says what it follows from. The story is not about how well schools teach. It is about who steers them, who is paid, and who was never asked.

Press Play the story, or click any chapter in the left panel to start there. Each chapter opens with a box. At its top is a one-line recap of the chapter before, so you know what you are carrying forward. Then comes the chapter's title and an introduction that explains how that part of the system works and why it matters. Under it, a short passage headed How the Slides Answer It says what each slide will add, in order. The box then fades and the slides play on the map, with each slide's text in the box on the right. Every slide begins by picking up from the one before, and explains each figure as soon as it gives it. Every box can be closed with its ×. The bar at the bottom has the controls: play and pause, one slide forward or back, the previous or next chapter, the reading speed, a button to hide or show the slide text, and a strip showing where you are in the whole story.

Slides marked Regional Example show the chapter's pattern in one country or region. Other slides cover every country at once: each country is shaded by a published figure, with a key. Hover over a country for its own figure and year. Others draw a whole network, such as every country the World Bank has lent to for education. The numbers in those slides are worked out from the source data, not written by hand.

What Is Drawn on Each Slide, and Why

Each slide has a short note headed On the map. It lists what is highlighted, which lines and points are drawn, and why those and no others. The rule is the same throughout: only the places named in the slide's own source are drawn. Where a source gives a figure for every country, every country is shaded. Where it names a few examples out of many, the note says they are examples. Slides are kept zoomed out so each place is seen in its part of the world.

The Organisations, and Why These Ones

The circles are 214 organisations. There are millions of schools, companies and offices in education; these were chosen by one test: is this body among the largest or most powerful of its kind, in the world or in its region, so that its decisions reach pupils far beyond its own doors? In practice that means:

  • International bodies and funds: the UN agencies with a mandate for education, the development banks that lend for it, the OECD, and the global funds that pay for schools in poorer countries.
  • Ministries and national boards: those in charge of the largest school systems in each region, plus the bodies that appear in the story.
  • Publishers, exam bodies and edtech: the largest sellers in each major language market, and the platforms most schools run on.
  • School operators, universities and for-profit colleges: the largest chains and groups by pupils or students.
  • Investors and owners: the funds and holding companies that own the bodies above.
  • Foundations, unions and cultural networks: the largest funders, the main teachers' unions, and the language institutes governments run abroad.

A switch in the legend, Show only the largest of each kind, hides the 27 smaller bodies that are on the map only because the story names them, such as a single school chain or one state's board. The list is not complete, and being on it says only that a body is a major part of education, not that it has done anything wrong. Each sits in its headquarters city, coloured by kind, as its own point at every zoom. Where several share a city they sit in a small ring around it. For-profit colleges and degree mills carry an extra ring. Click one to see what it is, who owns it, what it owns, and which chapters it appears in.

The Index and the Two Chapter Lists

Under the search box, the Index lists every organisation, every country the story names and every record in alphabetical order. Below it the chapters are listed twice, and the two lists are the same 26 chapters. The first is in story order, from the top of the system down. The second, Find Your Region in the Story, sorts them by where their slides take place.

Schools

The small dots are the schools themselves: all 2,336,677 schools in 221 countries and territories that Giga, the UNICEF and ITU project to map and connect the world's schools, has located. Each is coloured by whether Giga records it as connected to the internet: 366,201 are recorded as connected, 420,534 as not connected, and for the rest it is not known. Every school is drawn at every zoom; zoom in to see them apart, and hover over one for its name and level. Giga's count is not every school: the working estimate is six to seven million worldwide.

How to Read It

Countries are not shaded unless the story is playing. Outside the figures published for every country, any shading this map could offer would measure how much has been written down rather than how much is happening. A country the story does not name is a gap in the research. Being on this map as an organisation says only that an organisation is a major part of education, not that it has done anything wrong. The records inside the chapters are the evidence, and every one carries a link you can follow without taking this map's word for it.

The Method page sets out what counts as a chapter, how each slide is sourced, how the organisations were placed, where the school data comes from, and what is still missing.

What the Map Shows

Three layers. The story: how education is steered, supplied, owned and sold, told in order from the top of the system down. Organisations: the major bodies in education worldwide, at their headquarters. Schools: every school Giga has located. The documented records sit inside the story as evidence and can also be shown on their own.

What Counts as a Chapter

A chapter has to pass two questions. Does it reach a student wherever they are? It must describe how school works for people far from where any one episode happened. Does it show who steers, owns or is paid? A fact about how well or badly schools teach does not qualify by itself; nor does the plain fact that something is public or private. It qualifies when it shows the working of the system: who decides, who earns, and who was left out of the decision. A single takeover, a single law or a single news story is not a chapter. It can appear inside one, as evidence, when it shows the pattern.

How the Story Is Ordered

The order runs down the chain of command, because each layer is easier to understand once the layer above it is known. It starts with the international bodies that hold the plan, the money and the ranking. Then the national government, which works inside the limits those bodies set and holds the power to make things compulsory. Then the suppliers that governments buy rules, lessons and tests from. Then the owners of schools, who followed the suppliers in. Then software, the newest layer. Then what is sold after school. The last part gathers the cases where a pattern was reversed, and ends by showing every layer in one country. Each chapter has an introduction that explains how its layer works, then a short bridge that says how its slides answer the chapter's question in order. Each slide opens by picking up from the slide before. A one-line recap of each chapter is shown at the top of the next chapter's box, so no chapter has a separate closing box except the last. Where a pattern appears in several regions it is told once, with its regional cases as slides marked Regional Example.

How the Slides Are Built

Each slide is placed where it happened and carries its source. Where a slide rests on one of the map's documented records, the record's own source is used and the record is shown on the map while the slide plays. Each slide explains in plain words what a fact means straight after giving it, and turns large figures into something a reader can picture, such as a share out of ten. Those sentences are this map's reading of the facts; the facts themselves are the source's. Countries light up in the colour of the part they play and stay lit until the chapter ends. Lines are drawn between the places money, programmes, ownership or students move between. They show that something moved, not the route it took. One slide has no source of its own: the one that rings the government language networks, each of which carries its source on its own card.

Where a slide names countries, only the countries its source names are lit, and the note under the slide says so. The Global Partnership for Education slide lights all 94 partner countries listed on the fund's own website. The PISA slide lights the OECD's members and the partners its report names, not all 81 participants.

Slides That Cover Every Country

Slides that shade every country use the latest figure each source publishes for each country since 2012, so the year differs between countries and is given in each country's tooltip. Every country with a figure is shaded; nothing is left out or adjusted. The shades split the range into five bands, shown in the key. The highest and lowest countries named in the text are drawn from the 196 sovereign states, so that small territories with extreme figures do not crowd them out; the territories are still shaded. Two published figures are flagged in the text where they appear: Zimbabwe's government spending on education for 2020, given as 60% of national income, which is far outside the normal range; and China's PISA score, which covers four provinces, not the whole country.

  • UNESCO Institute for Statistics: private share of enrolment at each level, the gap in reading at age 15 between children who speak the test language at home and those who do not, government spending on education, what households pay per pupil, international students hosted and sent abroad, and the flows of students between every pair of countries. Where a country counts state-funded schools run by private bodies as private, as the United Kingdom does for its universities, the figure follows the country's own classification.
  • World Bank: learning poverty (the share of ten-year-olds who cannot read a simple text or are out of school, a measure the Bank launched with UNESCO's statistics office in 2019), pupils per teacher in primary school, and every education project in its projects database. Lending lines are drawn from Washington to each borrowing country, as total commitments since 1962. 58 projects are regional or multi-country and cannot be placed on one country, so they are counted in no country's line.
  • OECD: PISA 2018 mathematics scores, as republished in the World Bank's EdStats.
  • Giga: how many schools each country has on Giga's map, and the share recorded as connected where the connection status of at least 50 schools is known.
  • Turkish Maarif Foundation: its own world map of its schools, each at the coordinates it publishes (304 schools in 62 countries).
  • Confucius Institutes: the directory published by the Chinese International Education Foundation (589 sites in 159 countries).
  • Human Rights Watch: all 49 governments whose endorsed learning products it tested in 2022.
  • Global Partnership for Education: the partner countries listed on its website in November 2026.

The student-flow slide for the whole world draws the 523 flows of 2,000 students or more, which carry 80 per cent of the 6,975,775 students UNESCO counts as studying abroad; drawing all 12,219 at world scale would fill the globe. Each country's tooltip gives its full totals in both directions. The regional student-flow slides draw every flow, however small.

How the Organisations Were Chosen and Placed

The About box sets out the test for inclusion: the largest or most powerful bodies of each kind, in the world or in their region. An organisation is placed in its headquarters city. The bodies first researched for this map in detail are at their headquarters address; the rest at the city, which is said on each card. Where several sit in one city, they are spread around it by a fixed number of screen pixels so each can be clicked. No stored coordinate is changed. Marker colours change with the basemap so they stand off the ground beneath them.

Descriptions of organisations are kept neutral: what the body is and what part of education it touches. Where a body appears in the story, the slide says what it did and gives the source.

The School Data

The school dots come from Giga, the joint initiative of UNICEF and the International Telecommunication Union, through its data service: 2,336,677 schools in 221 countries and territories, downloaded in November 2026. Giga assembles school locations from about fifty governments, from OpenStreetMap and from its own model run on satellite imagery, and records whether each school is connected to the internet where that is known: 366,201 connected, 420,534 not connected, 1,549,942 unknown. The dots are drawn as Giga publishes them; this map does not correct, filter or add to them. Every school is drawn at every zoom. At wider views, schools that fall within the same fraction of a screen pixel are drawn as one dot, because they would be indistinguishable anyway; from zoom 9 each school is its own point with its name. Where a country has no dots, Giga has no published locations for it, which is not the same as having no schools.

Records

Each record rests on at least one of: a court or regulator's ruling, an official inquiry or truth commission, a company's own filing, a signed contract, an organisation's own published figures, a peer-reviewed study, or reporting with primary material behind it. Where the only source is a party to a dispute, the record says so. Where a company has answered, the answer is in the record.

Coverage

Two figures, both judgements rather than counts. Research so far, roughly 5 to 10 per cent, is how much of everything that could be documented about who controls schooling is on this map. Of your own school day, roughly 25 to 40 per cent, is how much of the machinery behind a pupil's day, the book, the exam, the device and account, the standards, the fees, the language and who owns the school, this map can account for. It varies by region:

What Was Left Out on Purpose

Figures about how well schools teach, such as how many children are out of school or reach a reading level, are not slides of their own, because this map is about who controls school, not how it performs. Two are kept where they show control: the World Bank's learning poverty measure, as the scorecard the lender itself wrote, and pupils per teacher, as the one thing the system does not sell.

What Is Missing

No chapters yet on credential inflation, on teachers' pay and conditions, on what university endowments invest in, on who is kept out of school by disability, migration status, gender or caste, on religious school systems, or on the learning built outside all of it. Geographically the story is thinnest in Central Asia, Southeast Asia and the Pacific. These are gaps in the research; nothing here should be read as saying those places are unaffected.

Corrections

If a slide, a record or an organisation's description is wrong, it should be corrected rather than defended. Every slide and card carries its source, so any single claim can be checked without taking this map's word for it.
